# agent-skills

One skill pack shared by several projects and agent harnesses (Claude Code,
opencode, Codex, Cursor and others).

## Instruction files

Everything that is not specific to one harness lives here in `AGENTS.md`:
layout, commands, workflow, conventions. `CLAUDE.md` holds only Claude Code
notes and imports this file with `@AGENTS.md`. Agents other than Claude treat
`CLAUDE.md` as read-only and put their notes here or in their own vendor file.
Keep this paragraph (and its twin in `CLAUDE.md`) when editing either file.

## Public repo: what may be committed (the user, 2026-11-08)

This repository is public. Anything sensitive, too specific to one person or
machine, or half-baked stays out. A new skill (or a change to one) is
committed only when it meets all of these:

1. **Generally useful** to many people, not just one project or one person.
2. **No machine or account details:** no user or account names, hostnames,
   personal email addresses, home-directory paths, private repo names or
   internal URLs. Use placeholders (`<user>`, `~`, `$HOME`, `%USERPROFILE%`,
   `user@example.com`) and paths relative to the skill.
3. **No secrets:** no passwords, tokens, API keys, private keys or
   credentials of any kind, not even expired or "test" ones.
4. **Reasonable quality** by the Agent Skills standard
   (https://agentskills.io/specification) and the obra/superpowers
   `writing-skills` checklist: a "Use when..." trigger description, tested
   against agents with and without the skill, concise, no narrative.
5. **Original to this repo:** skills that started elsewhere (third-party
   packs, even with local edits) stay out. Point to their upstream instead,
   and send improvements there as a PR. Check a skill's frontmatter
   (`metadata.author`, `license`) and footer for its origin before adding it
   (the user, 2026-11-08).

Before committing: run the tests (`tests/test_public_safety.py` catches the
mechanical cases of 2 and 3) **and** read the whole diff for anything the
patterns can't see. When in doubt, leave it out; keep personal or
project-specific skills in that project's own repo.

## Paths: no machine or account details

Everything committed must work for any account on any machine.

- Never write a user name, account name or machine name into the repo.
- Never write an absolute path that starts with a drive letter (`C:`, `D:`,
  ...) or with `/`. Start absolute paths from a standard location variable
  instead:
  - Windows prose: `%USERPROFILE%`, `%APPDATA%`, `%LOCALAPPDATA%`,
    `%ProgramFiles%`
  - PowerShell: `$env:USERPROFILE`, `$env:APPDATA`, `$env:LOCALAPPDATA`,
    `$env:ProgramFiles`, in double quotes (single quotes don't expand)
  - Linux/macOS: `~/`, `$HOME`; in CI, `$RUNNER_TEMP`
- Inside a skill, use paths relative to the skill's folder (`scripts/x.py`,
  `references/y.md`): the skill is installed in different places by
  different harnesses.
- Exceptions:
  - system locations that have no variable (`/Applications/...` on macOS)
  - verbatim upstream copies (`skills/*/references/`), which keep their own
    example paths
  - made-up fixture paths in `tests/`
- `tests/test_public_safety.py` fails on drive-letter paths and on home paths
  with a real-looking account name; other `/` paths need the diff review.

## Layout

Follows the layout of `obra/superpowers` (a popular pack that supports several
vendors' plugin formats):

- `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` - one folder per skill; `<name>` is lowercase with
  hyphens and equals the frontmatter `name`. Optional `references/` (Markdown
  the skill links to), `scripts/` (tools the skill runs; invoke them through
  their interpreter, e.g. `python scripts/x.py`).
- `tests/` - stdlib `python3` `unittest` tests. `test_skills.py` checks every
  skill (the frontmatter standard below, name = folder, single-line
  `description` starting "Use when", every `references/*.md` linked from
  `SKILL.md`, no nested `SKILL.md`); `test_public_safety.py` scans every tracked file for secrets,
  personal emails, account home paths and drive-letter paths; per-skill
  tests are `test_<skill-with-underscores>.py` and must start with
  `if not selected("<skill>"): raise unittest.SkipTest(...)` (from
  `tests/_select.py`; a test enforces it).
- `scripts/ci_changed_skills.py` - CI's selector: maps the files changed
  since the base commit to the skills to test (`skills/<name>/` or
  `tests/test_<name>.py` -> that skill; shared tests, `scripts/`, `.github/`
  -> all; notes -> none) and, with `--check-versions`, fails when an existing
  skill changed without a higher `metadata.version`.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` - runs on pushes to `main` and `skill/**`, and on
  PRs (opened, synchronize, reopened). Always runs the safety scan; runs the
  unit tests and the skills CLI check (`npx skills add . --list`) only for
  the selected skills (`SKILLS=<list>`; unset locally = all). No network in
  the tests.
- `skills/index.json` - generated opencode HTTP skill catalog (every skill's
  `name`, `metadata.version` and file list). Never hand-edit it:
  `python3 scripts/build_skills_index.py` writes it, `--check` reports a
  missing or stale file. On pushes to `main`, the CI job `skills-index`
  regenerates and commits it when `skills/` changed, it is missing, or it is
  stale (the user, 2026-11-08). opencode re-downloads a skill only when its
  version changes, which "Updating a skill" already requires.
- `docs/plans/` - finished plans (`YYYY-MM-<topic>.md`).
- `TODO.md` - open work. `BUGS.md` - upstream bugs (create when needed).

Run the tests from the repo root: `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v`.

## Skill frontmatter (the user, 2026-11-08)

Format: the Agent Skills specification,
https://agentskills.io/specification.md (index of all its pages:
https://agentskills.io/llms.txt). Every `SKILL.md` in this repo starts with
these fields, in this order:

```yaml
---
name: <skill-name>
description: <triggering conditions only, starting "Use when">
compatibility: <only if the skill needs an atypical environment>
license: MIT
metadata:
  author: Robert Stone
  source: https://github.com/rjstone/agent-skills
  version: "0.1.0"
---
```

- Required here: `name`, `description`, `license`, and `metadata` with
  `author`, `source` and `version`. Add co-authors to `author`, separated
  by commas.
- `version` is a quoted `"X.Y.Z"` string (metadata values are strings).
  New skills start at `"0.1.0"`.
- `compatibility` (1-500 characters) only when it's worthwhile: system
  packages or tools that usually aren't installed (Xvfb, ImageMagick,
  tkinter), network access a script needs, or one intended product. Leave
  it out for things nearly everyone has (Python, git, a shell).
- License and attribution live only in the frontmatter: no license or
  "maintained by" prose in the body. One exception: an optional `## Credits`
  section, last in the file, of one or two plain sentences crediting an
  inspiration or prior idea (not authorship or license; the user, 2026-11-08).

## Skills

- `opencode-build` - opencode v2 Build docs (plugins, client, SDK) cached as
  Markdown in `references/`, with `scripts/refresh_references.py` to update
  them and `ERRATA.md` for known doc mistakes. Never hand-edit the downloaded
  `references/` pages (a test compares each file with its hash in
  `references/manifest.json`). Our own additions go in `references/X.local.md`
  beside the page `X.md` they supplement (the user, 2026-11-09). Where they
  go, their style and the scripts that print type declarations
  (`scripts/dts_decls.py`, `scripts/client_outline.py`) are in the skill's
  `MAINTAINING.md`, which `SKILL.md` only points to: most uses of the skill
  never maintain it (the user, 2026-11-10).
  Started in the project that first needed it; that copy stays until this
  repo is set up and tested (the user, 2026-11-08).
- `timestamp` - `/timestamp [start|end|both|on|off]` prints a tool-read
  time with a delta at the start and/or end of each turn.
- `concept-parable` - explains a concept as a fable whose governing
  condition drives the plot, with a late reveal and a mapping.
- `capturing-tk-screenshots-headless` - run a Tk GUI on Xvfb and capture it
  with ImageMagick; `scripts/grab_stable.py` waits until drawing settles.
  App-specific notes (e.g. Thonny config) stay in that app's projects
  (the user, 2026-11-08).
- `pygameturbo` - Pygame Turbo (pgturbo) help and beginner teaching. Its
  `references/` are verbatim copies of the upstream docs sources
  (`doc/*.rst` in Mambouna/pgturbo, LGPL-3.0, license in
  `references/COPYING`, notice in `references/README.md`), pinned to the
  commit in `references/manifest.json` by `scripts/refresh_references.py`
  (stdlib; `--ref <branch|tag|sha>`, `--check`). Never hand-edit them; the
  skill's own text is MIT (the user, 2026-11-10).
- `thonny-plugin` - Thonny IDE plugin authoring: `thonnycontrib`
  discovery, the per-OS plugin folder (from Thonny 5.0.1's
  `thonny/__init__.py` and `misc_utils.py`), UI-thread rule, test ladder,
  and `references/api-5.0.1.md` (every name checked against the 5.0.1
  package). Re-verify against the installed Thonny when it changes
  (the user, 2026-11-10).
- `provider-onboarding` - provider card plus opencode / fast-agent / curl
  snippets for an LLM provider or model; `scripts/lookup.py` reads
  models.dev data merged with `references/providers-overrides.json` (entries
  carry a `verified` date and `source`; re-verify before trusting old ones).
- `opencode-cli` - opencode v2 CLI docs (commands, `cli.json`, keybinds,
  themes, web UI, ACP) cached like `opencode-build`, with its own refresh
  script copy and `ERRATA.md`.
- `opencode-api` - opencode v2 server HTTP API: the published OpenAPI spec
  cached in `references/openapi.json`, searched with `scripts/api_lookup.py`
  (too large to read whole); calls via `opencode api` or Basic auth.

## Decisions (the user, 2026-11-08)

- **Formats:** ship for skills.sh (`npx skills add rjstone/agent-skills`) first.
  It discovers `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` directly, so no manifest is needed.
  Other formats are in `TODO.md`.
- **One pack**, not a marketplace of separate plugins.
- **No symlinks** (Windows needs admin or Developer Mode for them). Keep one
  real `skills/` tree; a format that needs files elsewhere points its manifest
  at `skills/`, or a script generates the copy. Never link.
- **Tests:** stdlib `python3` `unittest` plus GitHub Actions.
- **Git:** repo-level changes (notes, tests, CI, tooling) go straight to
  `main`; use a branch only for large ones. Skills follow "Adding a skill" and
  "Updating a skill" below.
- **Versioning:** no releases yet; skills.sh installs from the default branch.
  Add versioning with the first plugin format that has a version field.

## Adding a skill (the user, 2026-11-08)

1. Branch `main` to `skill/<skill-name>`.
2. Commit all of the skill's files on that branch, in the locations and
   format this file requires (`skills/<name>/`, its `tests/test_<name>.py` if
   any, the frontmatter standard, the public-repo criteria).
3. Run the tests on the skill (CI also runs on every push to `skill/**`).
4. Ask for review and wait for it.
5. When approved, **squash-merge** `skill/<skill-name>` into `main`: the
   initial add of a skill is the only squash.
6. Delete the merged branch, or ask the user to.

## Updating a skill (the user, 2026-11-08)

1. Branch to `update/<skill-name>`.
2. Always bump `metadata.version`, roughly semver: **major** for breaking or
   big changes, **minor** when files are added, **patch** for edits that add
   no files. CI fails a change to an existing skill without a higher version.
3. Commit the changes to the branch.
4. Open a PR for the branch (CI runs on the PR and on each push to it).
5. When done, merge with a **merge commit** (no squash, no fast-forward) and
   delete the branch.

## Formats (status)

- skills.sh (`npx skills`) - **supported** (https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills,
  discovery rules in its `docs/creating-skills.md`).
- opencode HTTP skill catalog - **supported**: add
  `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rjstone/agent-skills/main/skills/` to
  `skills` in `opencode.json(c)`; opencode reads `skills/index.json` there.
  Not `https://github.com/...` (a web page; opencode gets 403 for
  `index.json`). Explicit `skills` entries take precedence over local copies.
- Claude Code plugin (`.claude-plugin/plugin.json` / `marketplace.json`) - TODO.
- Claude desktop/web plugins - TODO.
- opencode v1/v2 plugins - TODO.

## Standing policies

- **Dependencies:** prefer the language's standard library and no install
  step, so any harness, container or fresh machine runs the code as is. Add a
  dependency only when it clearly earns its keep, and note why here.
- **Secrets:** never print, `cat` or otherwise read a key file, token or
  passphrase into context, and never put one in a commit, log or message;
  check existence with `ls -l` or `wc -c` only. If one reaches the context,
  say so at once and tell the user to rotate it. Commit secrets only
  encrypted (e.g. GnuPG symmetric `<name>.pgp` plus a small encrypt/decrypt
  script); decrypted copies are git-ignored and mode 600.
- **Pushes:** if a push is rejected with "fetch first", rebase your unpushed
  commits onto the remote (`git pull --rebase`) and push again. Never
  force-push over someone else's commits.
- **Notes:** when a session finds a new fact, quirk or workaround, write it
  here (or in `CLAUDE.md` if Claude-only) before the session ends. Mark the
  user's decisions with who and when, e.g. "(the user, 2026-11-08)".
- **Plans:** finished plans go in `docs/plans/YYYY-MM-<topic>.md`.
  "Archiving the plan" means: once the work is done, copy the working plan
  there, remove the original, commit and push.

# Claude Code notes

Only Claude-specific notes go here: Claude Code tools, subagents, settings,
hooks, slash commands and quirks of the Claude Code (web) container.
Everything shared lives in `AGENTS.md`, imported above. Agents other than
Claude treat this file as read-only. Keep this paragraph (and its twin in
`AGENTS.md`) when editing either file.

## Config that persists

On Claude Code on the web the container is rebuilt each session, so anything
only in `~/.claude` is lost. Persistent Claude config goes in this repo's
`.claude/` (settings, agents, commands). If something must sit at user scope,
link that one item into `~/.claude/` (re-create it each session, e.g. from a
SessionStart hook). Never link `~/.claude` itself into the repo or the other
way: it holds credentials and transcripts. Skills stay in `skills/` (no
symlinks, see AGENTS.md).

Claude Code keeps the working plan in `~/.claude/plans/`, which disappears
with a cloud container: archive it to `docs/plans/` before the session ends.

## Claude Code on the web: skills CLI

- `npx skills find <query>` returns "No skills found" for every query in the
  web container (even `react`): its search service isn't reachable there.
  To find a skill, identify the source repo (e.g. a plugin's
  `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, or Anthropic's
  `anthropics/claude-plugins-official`) and run
  `npx skills add <owner/repo> --list`, which works.

## Claude Code on the web: git

- The session's git proxy refuses deleting remote branches (HTTP 403 on
  `git push origin --delete`), and the GitHub tools here have no delete. No
  need: GitHub deletes a PR's branch when it is merged (repo setting; the
  user, 2026-11-10). After a merge, delete only the local branch.
- The clone is shallow (`--depth 1`) and tracks only `main`. A branch you
  push later gets no `origin/<branch>` ref, even with `git push -u`
  ("upstream branch ... not stored as a remote-tracking branch"), so `git
  status` and the session's stop hook report it as unpushed with no remote
  branch although the push worked. Before the first push of a new branch:
  `git config --add remote.origin.fetch '+refs/heads/<branch>:refs/remotes/origin/<branch>'`,
  then `git push -u origin <branch>`. Already pushed: add the same line,
  `git fetch origin <branch>`, `git branch -u origin/<branch>`.

## Delegating to subagents

- Hand long, mechanical runs (batch jobs, long waits, log sweeps) to a cheap
  subagent (usually Haiku, only the tools it needs) that returns a short
  report.
- Two or more independent problems with no shared state: use
  `dispatching-parallel-agents` (obra/superpowers), one subagent per problem
  in the same response, then verify everything yourself.
- Larger plans with several tasks: use `subagent-driven-development`.
- When the opencode subagent tools are available, read `delegate-to-opencode`
  before delegating; it suits mechanical, well-specified jobs. Keep
  judgment-heavy work and anything touching secrets on native subagents.
- Parallel code changes: give each agent its own worktree
  (`using-git-worktrees`). Read-only or non-overlapping work doesn't need it.
- On the web, when the egress proxy injects a host's real credentials, set
  the key variables a client needs to a placeholder (e.g. `proxy-injected`);
  never ask for or write in a real value.

# Capturing Tk screenshots headless

## Overview
Run the GUI on a virtual X server (Xvfb) and capture with ImageMagick `import`. There is no window manager: no title bars, every window opens at 0,0, and `import -window <id>` copies whatever is on screen in that window's rectangle, including other windows covering it.

## Before you start
- Use a Python **that has tkinter**: `python -c "import tkinter"`. Sandbox system `python3` often lacks it; a venv with Thonny or `python3-tk` has it.
- Tools: `Xvfb`, `xvfb-run`, `import`, `convert` (ImageMagick). Often missing: `xdotool`, `xwininfo`, `scrot`. Don't plan on them.

## Recipe A: your own widget or test window
```bash
xvfb-run -a -s "-screen 0 1600x1200x24" PY capture.py
```
```python
import subprocess, tkinter as tk
root = tk.Tk(); root.withdraw()
wins = [make_window_1(root), make_window_2(root)]      # your Toplevels
for i, w in enumerate(wins, 1):
    for o in wins:                                       # show ONE window at a time
        o.deiconify() if o is w else o.withdraw()
    root.update(); root.after(300); root.update()        # let Tk finish drawing
    subprocess.run(["import", "-window", str(w.winfo_id()), f"win{i}.png"], check=True)
root.destroy()
```
Skip `mainloop()` in capture scripts; `update()` draws everything.

## Recipe B: a real application (Thonny, IDLE, ...)
1. `Xvfb :77 -screen 0 1200x800x24 &` (explicit display number, screen = desired image size).
2. Give the app a **throwaway config dir** with theme, font size and window geometry preset to fill the screen at 0,0 (most apps take a config-directory environment variable or option; check the app's docs). An empty config dir often opens a first-run or welcome dialog instead of the main window: preset the settings that skip it. Never touch the user's real config.
3. Open a file with real content so themes, syntax colors and fonts are visible.
4. Launch with `DISPLAY=:77 ... &`, then wait for it to settle instead of sleeping a guessed time:
   `python3 scripts/grab_stable.py :77 out.png` (waits until the screen is non-blank and stops changing, tolerates a blinking cursor; `--crop WxH+X+Y`, `--timeout`).
5. Kill the app, then Xvfb. Read the app's log for "Could not find ..." warnings.

## Always
- **Open every PNG yourself** (whatever image-viewing tool your harness has) before reporting, and describe what it actually shows: a capture that ran without errors can still be black, half-drawn or the wrong window.
- Keep scratch files out of the project; hand finished images to the person with your harness's file-sharing mechanism.
- Captures are 1:1 pixels at Tk's 1x rendering.
- Running in Claude Code? Also read `claude-code.md` for its tool names and container notes.

## Common mistakes
| Symptom | Cause / fix |
|---|---|
| Black or another window inside a capture | Windows overlap at 0,0: show one at a time, or place with `geometry("+X+Y")` and crop `-window root` |
| Capture of a half-built window | Missing `update()`/`after()`, or fixed sleep too short: use `grab_stable.py` |
| App ignored the theme | Wrong theme name or UI vs editor theme mixed up; check log |
| App at an offset on a black screen | Geometry not preset; screen size not matched |
| Emoji gray/outline, extra blank cell after ⬅️ | Tk 8.6 draws no color emoji; U+FE0F takes a cell. `fc-list ":charset=274c" family` shows which font supplies a glyph |
| `OSError: AF_UNIX path too long` at launch | The app's socket path (under a long config or runtime dir) exceeds the ~108-byte limit: use a shorter dir, or set `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` to one |
| Fonts differ from the user's OS | Sandbox fonts (e.g. DejaVu) ≠ Windows Consolas/Segoe; say so |

# Concept Parable

Given a concept, subject, or domain, write a short fable that dramatizes the concept's *mechanics*
indirectly through story, keeps the concept's identity hidden until a late reveal, and then explains
— concisely — how each part of the story stood for a part of the concept.

The value of a good concept-parable is that a reader meets the *shape* of an idea before they meet
its name, so the name later lands on a structure they already understand. That only works if the
structure in the story is truly the concept's structure. Most of this skill is about getting that
right.

## If the subject is a broad domain

Pick one specific, interesting concept from it. Avoid the single most commonly-cited concept in that
domain unless it is genuinely the best fit — the obvious pick is usually the one the reader has
already met head-on. When choosing among several candidates with no clear winner, vary your choice
rather than always defaulting to the same instinct; pseudo-random selection is fine if it helps you
break a tie.

## The core tension — resolve it before you start

"Illustrate the mechanics *fully*" and "keep the concept *hidden*" sound contradictory. They are not,
once you separate **structure** from **identity**:

- Render the **structure** faithfully and completely — the parts, how they relate, and the
  conditions under which the relation holds — so that a reader could reverse-engineer the concept
  from the story alone.
- Hide only the **identity** — the concept's name and its domain's vocabulary. Use no technical
  labels, jargon, or telltale terms until the reveal.

You are hiding the *label on the box*, never the *contents of the box*.

## Before writing: map three kinds of parts

Forced, creaky parables almost always come from mapping only nouns — thing-to-thing — and neglecting
the rest. A concept has three kinds of parts. Enumerate all three, then invent one story stand-in for
each:

1. **Entities** — the things involved. These become characters and objects. This part is easy and
   rarely where parables fail.
2. **Relations and operations** — what acts on what, what transforms into what, what depends on what.
   These become the events and actions of the plot.
3. **The governing condition** — the constraint under which the whole thing holds: the right angle,
   the convergence requirement, the conserved quantity, the maintained invariant, the assumption that
   licenses the inference. This is usually the actual *point* of the concept, and it is the single
   easiest thing to accidentally render as scenery.

Aim for roughly one story-element per real-element — a clean, near-bijective mapping with no orphans
and no decoration. Prefer a few correspondences that carry weight over an exhaustive set that turns
the story into a puzzle.

## The load-bearing check

Before drafting, ask one question about the governing condition: **does it do real work in the plot?**

If the story would read the same with the constraint removed or violated, the constraint is
decorative — and the parable will feel forced, because the concept's heart is missing while its
surface is present. Rebuild so that when the constraint is *absent*, the story visibly fails. That
failure is frequently the most illuminating beat you can offer, because it shows the reader what the
constraint is *for*.

## Tone and shape

- Fable-like and legible. The story should be *easier* to parse than the concept, never a dense
  allegory that is harder to decode than the thing it explains.
- Keep the subject hidden or ambiguous for most of the story. No winks, no giveaway vocabulary.
- A few paragraphs. It must work as a story first — satisfying even to a reader who never decodes it.
- The strongest reveals are a **recontextualizing turn**: a final image or line that makes the reader
  see the whole story *was* the concept all along, rather than a label bolted onto the end. Reach for
  that when the material allows; don't force it if a plainer reveal serves better.

## After the story: the mapping

Stop the story, then write a separate explanation:

- Name the concept plainly.
- Map each story element to what it stood for — entities, relations, and *especially* the governing
  condition. Make the condition's role explicit; it is the part the reader most needs named.
- Keep it no longer than necessary to communicate the mapping. This is a key, not an essay.
- Optional closing beat: one honest line on where the analogy simplifies or breaks down. This builds
  trust and marks the boundary of the metaphor so the reader knows how far to carry it.

## Silent self-check before shipping

Verify these in your reasoning, not on the page:

- Could a reader who does not know the concept reconstruct its mechanics from the story alone?
- Does every essential part appear — entities, relations, and the governing condition?
- Does the constraint do load-bearing work, or is it scenery?
- Does it read as a story first, not a cipher?
- Is the reveal genuinely late, and ideally a turn rather than a tacked-on label?

If any answer is no, fix it before returning the parable.

## Domain notes: what tends to go invisible

Different domains hide their load-bearer in different places. Use these hints to find the part most at
risk of becoming scenery, and the framing that tends to resist forcing. Extend this table as new
domains come up.

| Domain | What tends to go invisible | Framing that resists forcing |
|---|---|---|
| Mathematics | the governing condition (a right angle, a convergence or invertibility assumption) | a physical action or process, not a static container of "stuff" |
| Physics / chemistry | the *mechanism* of change (conserved quantities are the easy part) | a process unfolding over time |
| Biology / evolution | the selective pressure — the filter — not the surviving trait | many trials run against an environment that filters them |
| Economics / game theory | incentives and information asymmetry (not the payoff numbers) | agents deciding under what they can and cannot see |
| CS / algorithms | the invariant preserved across every step | a repeated routine bound by one rule it must never break |
| Statistics | the assumption that licenses the inference | what goes wrong the moment that assumption quietly fails |

## A worked contrast — why the constraint carries the parable

Take **negative feedback** (a system that self-corrects toward a set point).

- **Forced:** a gardener waters the plants each day. Watering illustrates "an action," but nothing in
  the story ties the *size* of the action to *how far things have drifted* — the story reads
  identically whether or not any feedback exists. The concept's heart is missing; only its surface
  (someone doing something regularly) is present.
- **Faithful:** the response *scales with the deviation* — a small drift brings a small correction, a
  large drift a large one — and when that proportionality is broken (the corrector overreacts, or
  reacts late), the system visibly overshoots and oscillates. Now the governing relation is doing the
  work, the failure mode teaches what the constraint is for, and a reader could recover "negative
  feedback" from the mechanics without ever being told the name.

The difference between the two is not vocabulary or polish. It is whether the governing condition was
mapped and made load-bearing, or left as scenery.

Originally inspired by an idea expressed by Amanda Askell of Anthropic in a video interview.

# opencode server API (v2)

## Overview

opencode v2 moved every server route under `/api/` (`POST /api/session`,
`GET /api/event`, `GET /api/info`), so the v1 routes you remember (`/session`,
`/event`, `/global/health`, `/doc`) are probably wrong. **Do not write opencode
API calls from memory.** Look each one up in the cached OpenAPI spec,
`references/openapi.json` (~880 KB, 170 operations): search it with the script
instead of reading it.

```bash
python scripts/api_lookup.py --tags                  # areas and operation counts
python scripts/api_lookup.py --list session          # operations in a tag (or matching text)
python scripts/api_lookup.py --op session.prompt     # params (with style), body, responses, opencode api + curl lines
python scripts/api_lookup.py --op POST /api/session  # same, by method and path
python scripts/api_lookup.py --schema Session        # one schema
python scripts/api_lookup.py --grep "fork session"   # words in ids, paths, summaries
```

Paths are relative to this skill's folder. `--depth N` limits how far `$ref`s
expand (default 3; use 1 for large bodies). When the spec and `ERRATA.md`
disagree, `ERRATA.md` wins.

## Calling the server

- **Easiest:** `opencode api <operationId>` (or `opencode api GET /api/...`)
  talks to the running server with its connection and password already set:
  `opencode api session.list --param limit=10`,
  `opencode api session.create --data '{"title": "x"}'`. `--op` prints this
  form for each operation, and a `curl` line to adapt for other clients.
- **Other clients:** HTTP Basic auth, user `opencode`, the server password
  (`OPENCODE_PASSWORD`, or set it with `opencode service set password`):
  `curl -u opencode:$OPENCODE_PASSWORD http://127.0.0.1:<port>/api/info`.
  `opencode service status` prints the address. Never print or log the
  password. Details: https://opencode.ai/docs/cli/web (Markdown: same URL + `.md`).
- `GET /api/info` (`server.info`) returns the version, URLs and paths: a
  cheap first call to check the connection.
- The running server does not serve its own spec (no route for it; v1's
  `/doc` is gone, checked 2026-11-08). The published copy is
  https://opencode.ai/docs/openapi.json, cached here.
- Events: `GET /api/event` (`event.subscribe`) is a `text/event-stream`;
  filter with the `types` query parameter. It is volatile: a slow reader is
  dropped, and events during a disconnect are lost.
- **Location** (72 of 170 operations take it): the query parameter
  `location` is an object (`style: deepObject`; `--op` flags it and prints
  the URL form): `?location[directory]=<url-encoded dir>` (`curl -g`, or
  encode the brackets as `%5B`/`%5D`). On those operations a plain
  `?directory=` is ignored (the server's default location answers; a few
  others, like `session.list`, have a real `directory` filter of their
  own), and `?location=<dir>` → 400 `InvalidRequestError`
  "Expected object at [\"location\"]". `opencode api` fills it in for the
  current directory. Checked 2026-11-10 against opencode 2.2.6.
- **Plugin RPC:** `POST /api/rpc/{rpcID}/{method}` (`rpc.call`) wraps the
  argument: body `{"input": <value>}` → `{"output": <value>}`. `rpcID` is the
  id in the plugin's `Rpc.define`. A bare argument as the body →
  `rpc.invalid_input` "Expected object".
- **Throwaway server** (tests, sandboxes): `opencode serve --hostname
  127.0.0.1 --port <n> --print-logs` prints `server password <value>` at
  startup; point `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, `XDG_DATA_HOME`, `XDG_CACHE_HOME` and
  `XDG_STATE_HOME` at a temp folder to keep it off your real setup. A
  location's plugins load in the background after its first request, so
  plugin-provided agents, skills, references and MCP servers appear a few
  seconds later.

## Keeping it current

- `references/openapi.json` is a verbatim copy; **never edit it**. Refresh with
  `python scripts/refresh_references.py` (`--check` reports staleness without
  writing). The docs page https://opencode.ai/docs/api/ is generated from the
  same file.
- Found a mistake (the spec contradicts the running server)? Add an entry to
  `ERRATA.md` with the request, the response and the date.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| v1 routes (`/session/{id}/message`, `/event`, `/global/health`) | Look up the v2 operation: `--grep`, then `--op` |
| Reading `openapi.json` directly | `api_lookup.py`; the file is far too large for context |
| curl without auth | `-u opencode:<password>`, or use `opencode api` |
| Guessing a request body | `--op <id>` shows the schema; `--schema <Name>` for nested types |
| `?directory=<dir>` or `?location=<dir>` | `?location[directory]=<dir>` (deep-object query) |
| RPC call with the bare argument as body | `{"input": <value>}` |

# Provider onboarding

Turn "add support for `<provider>`'s `<model>`" into a verified-where-possible provider card and config snippets. The card is only as good as its sources, so every field is labeled with where it came from and anything inferred is said to be inferred.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the request** into a provider name, a model name, or both. "Add the Y model" with no provider is valid; the lookup lists every provider serving it.
2. **Run the lookup** (stdlib Python, no installs):
   ```bash
   python3 scripts/lookup.py --provider "<provider>" --model "<model>"
   python3 scripts/lookup.py --model "<model>"            # who serves this model?
   python3 scripts/lookup.py --list-providers             # browse
   python3 scripts/lookup.py -p X -m Y --format json      # machine-readable
   ```
   Paths are relative to this skill's directory. It reads `https://models.dev/api.json` and `https://models.opencode.ai/api.json` (override with `--url`, env `MODELS_DEV_URLS`, or `--file api.json`), merges `references/providers-overrides.json`, and caches for an hour. `--all-types` includes specialized model types hidden by default.
3. **Handle failure** by reading the lookup's message, then `references/data-sources.md`. In order: GitHub read of `anomalyco/models.dev` (`providers/<id>/provider.toml`), ask the user to upload `api.json` (`--file`), ask them to allow `models.dev` and `models.opencode.ai` in their agent's network settings (on claude.ai: Settings > Capabilities), or web-search the provider's docs. If the network refuses a host, say so plainly; do not hunt for a workaround.
4. **Provider not in any database?** Use manual mode after finding the docs: `--name X --base-url https://api.x.com/v1 --env-var X_API_KEY --model-id y`. It generates the same card and snippets.
5. **Deliver the card** (below), then the snippets the user's tooling needs, then the operator checklist.

## What the card must contain

- Base URL, API-key env var, protocol (OpenAI chat, Responses, Anthropic messages), docs URL
- Model id exactly as the API expects it, context/output limits, price per 1M tokens (omit if none published)
- Other providers serving the same model, with base URL and price, when the user hasn't pinned a provider
- Sign-up / key page candidates with confidence
- Hosts that must be allowlisted in any sandboxed agent
- A source tag per field: models.dev, override table (with verified date), inferred, manual, or MISSING

## Sign-up page inference

models.dev has no sign-up field, so the lookup infers. The rule: if the API lives at `api.modelprovider.com`, then `modelprovider.com` is probably where sign-up or subscribe links are.

- Apex of the API host: medium confidence. Apex of the docs host, if different: medium.
- Hosts on shared infrastructure (googleapis.com, amazonaws.com, azure.com, workers.dev, vercel.app, ...) get no apex guess, because the apex belongs to the cloud, not the provider. Say that and search the docs instead.
- The models.dev `doc` URL is low confidence; it is documentation, not necessarily sign-up.
- Never present an inferred URL as verified. Say "likely: <url>" and name the basis. Common paths to try by hand, all unverified: `/signup`, `/login`, `/dashboard`, `/keys`, `/api-keys`, `/console`. If a browser or fetch tool is available and the user wants confirmation, check the page and report what is really there.
- When a URL is confirmed, suggest adding it to `signup_url` in `references/providers-overrides.json` so it stops being a guess.

## Snippets generated

- **opencode v2** provider block with `{env:VAR}` substitution and top-level `model`. The `package` value comes from the data when present; otherwise it is `@opencode/ai/providers/openai-compatible` for OpenAI-compatible providers, or a flagged guess. Tell the user to confirm with `opencode debug config`.
- **fast-agent** `generic:` config using `base_url` and `api_key: "${VAR}"`, plus a `fast-agent go --model generic.<id> --message ...` smoke test.
- **curl** smoke test (OpenAI-style `/chat/completions` with a Bearer env var, or Anthropic `/messages` with `x-api-key` and `anthropic-version`); for unknown protocols it points at the docs instead of guessing.
- **env var** export line. Never ask the user to paste a key into chat, and never print one.

## Operator checklist (end every card with this)

1. Get an API key from the sign-up candidate (verify the page first).
2. Allowlist the hosts from the card in the agent's network settings.
3. Provide the key as an env var (or a placeholder if an egress proxy injects it).
4. Run the curl smoke test; a 200 with text is the real confirmation.
5. Record what was verified and the date; offer to add or fix an override entry.

## Honesty rules

- Date-stamp the lookup. Prices and model lists change; models.dev may lag the provider.
- A model name the user gives (or you remember) may be retired or renamed. Check the provider's
  models list or changelog before putting it in config, and say what replaced it.
- `UNVERIFIED author knowledge` in a source tag means it came from the seed override table, not a live check. Say so.
- A model with `status: deprecated/alpha/beta` or `experimental` gets a visible note.
- If matches were ambiguous (the lookup prints a warning), name the alternatives instead of silently choosing.
- The schema in `references/data-sources.md` was read from repo source, not live responses. If a live response differs, trust it and say so.

## Extending

Add verified providers to `references/providers-overrides.json` (fields: `base_url`, `env`, `hosts`, `signup_url`, `docs`, `headers`, `quirks`, `verified`, `source`). Quirks that burned someone belong there (free-tier limits, required headers, single-protocol models).

# Pygame Turbo

Pygame Turbo (`pgturbo`) is a fast-moving fork of Pygame Zero for
education: no event loop, no boilerplate. A game is a script that defines
hook functions (`draw()`, `update()`, `on_key_down()`, ...) and uses

Zero or an older Turbo: **read the matching reference before answering
anything detailed.**

commit in `references/manifest.json`; each page's online URL is in the
manifest too. License: [`references/README.md`](references/README.md).

Not vendored (read online at https://pgturbo.readthedocs.io/): the
example-game walkthroughs, the changelog, other libraries, contributing.
When you point a learner to a page, give its online URL from the manifest.

## Running a game

Outside an IDE, `pgtrun game.py` runs a script. Inside an IDE (Thonny,
IDLE, VS Code, ...) the script must import `pgtrun` first and call
`pgtrun.go()` last, so plain "Run" works
(`references/deep_dives/installation_and_running.rst`):

```python
import pgtrun

WIDTH = 300
HEIGHT = 300

def draw():
    screen.fill((128, 0, 0))

pgtrun.go()
```

`pgtrun` is Turbo's; `pgzrun` is Pygame Zero's. Don't mix them up:
Pygame Zero is older and better represented in training data. Turbo is
otherwise backward-compatible with Pygame Zero and adds features such as
flipbook animation and spritesheets.

## Common pitfalls

- Movement and physics belong in `update()`; `draw()` only paints.
- Hook arguments are passed by position and count:
  `on_mouse_down()`, `on_mouse_down(pos)` and `on_mouse_down(pos, button)`
  all work, but the order is fixed (`deep_dives/hooks.rst`).
- `draw()` takes no arguments; `update()` may take `dt`.
- An Actor's position is its anchor point, which defaults to the center,
  not the top-left corner.
- Images, sounds and music load by name from `images/`, `sounds/` and
  `music/` next to the script, always **without** file extension.
- Key names are attributes of `keyboard` and `keys`; check the exact names
  in `references/references/keyboard.rst`.

## Teaching a beginner

1. Ask what the game should do or what they tried; look at their code and
   any error.
2. When they start a new game, suggest a folder for it (no spaces in the
   name), and let them create it.
3. Start every explanation with which hooks the game needs and what work
   happens in each.
4. Check the exact API detail in `references/` before explaining it.
5. One small step at a time: name the hook or object, show a minimal
   snippet in chat, have them type it, run it and look.
6. Debug by prediction: "what do you expect after this change?", then run.
7. Let the learner install packages themselves (in Thonny: Tools > Manage
   packages); name the package rather than installing it.
8. Keep project facts (the game, its files, assets) in the project's own
   notes, not here: these docs describe the library, not their game.

A good order of first projects: a window with a bouncing ball, one actor
moved by the keyboard, collisions and a score, a scrolling background with
a spawner, sprite animation frames, sound and music, a saved high score
(`references/references/storage.rst`).

## Keeping references current

Never edit `references/`. Refresh from upstream with
`python scripts/refresh_references.py --ref main` (or a tag or commit);
`--check` reports edited or missing files offline, and with `--ref` also
whether upstream moved on. Then review the diff and update the table above
if pages were added, moved or removed.

# Thonny plugin authoring

Thonny discovers 3rd-party plugins at startup: any module or package under
the `thonnycontrib` namespace exposing a parameterless `load_plugin()`,
which Thonny calls exactly once. Everything else is convention around that.

## Layout

```text
thonnycontrib/
    __init__.py          # empty (namespace marker; a regular package works,
                         # but then this directory shadows namespace installs
                         # anywhere earlier on sys.path)
    my_plugin/
        __init__.py      # defines load_plugin()
```

`load_plugin()` registers with the workbench — typically
`get_workbench().add_command(...)` and/or `get_workbench().add_view(...)`.
Keep a module-level reference to anything that must outlive the call
(servers, threads); Thonny keeps only what you bind or thread yourself.

## Install location (the failure that matters)

Thonny's interpreter runs **isolated** (`no_user_site=1`,
`ignore_environment=1`, `isolated=1` — confirm with
`<thonny python> -c "import sys; print(sys.flags)"`). Its plugin loader
only looks in Thonny's own plugin folder:

- `<Thonny user data folder>/plugins/` plus the user-site layout of
  Thonny's Python: `PythonXY\site-packages` on Windows,
  `lib/pythonX.Y/site-packages` on Linux, `lib/python/site-packages` for a
  macOS framework Python. Put `thonnycontrib/` inside that.
- The user data folder: `%APPDATA%\Thonny` (Windows), `~/Library/Thonny`
  (macOS), `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/Thonny` or `~/.config/Thonny` (Linux);
  `user_data` beside the program for a portable Thonny; `THONNY_USER_DIR`
  overrides all of them. Tools > "Open Thonny data folder..." opens it.
- Example (Windows, Thonny 5.0.1 with Python 3.14):
  `%APPDATA%\Thonny\plugins\Python314\site-packages\thonnycontrib\`
- **NOT** the interpreter's user-site (e.g.
  `%APPDATA%\Python\Python314\site-packages`): it is not on Thonny's path,
  so a plugin installed there silently never loads — no error, no menu
  item, nothing in the log.
- After copying, strip `__pycache__` and **restart Thonny** (full quit;
  the new process is what loads it). Verify with the menu item, not the
  import.

## UI-thread rule

HTTP threads, background threads, and timers must never touch Tk or
Thonny objects directly. Marshal with `get_workbench().after(0, fn)` and
block the worker on a `queue.Queue` for the result (10 s timeout is plenty).
Read-only Tk getters also count — call them on the UI thread.

## Test ladder (each step proves strictly more)

1. **Syntax/import** with Thonny's bundled interpreter (Windows:
   `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Thonny\python.exe`; never a bare `python`,
   which on Windows may be the Microsoft Store stub). Proves the file
   parses and `load_plugin` exists. Proves nothing about loading. Running
   the file directly (`python.exe plugin.py`) proves even less — it never
   calls `load_plugin`.
2. **Restart Thonny, check the Tools menu** (or view) for your item. Absent
   item = wrong install location (see above) or an exception at load —
   the latter IS logged (`frontend.log` in the user data folder; look for
   "Failed loading plugin"). No log error + no item = location problem.
3. **Exercise it live** against the running Thonny (click it; or call its
   HTTP endpoint if it serves one). Import checks cannot replace this.

## API reference

Verified against Thonny 5.0.1 — do not trust memory or newer upstream;
signatures drift (e.g. `get_current_breakpoints()` keys by
`get_filename()` in 5.0.1). Re-verify anything not listed with
`inspect.signature`/`inspect.getsource` against the installed `thonny`
package (Windows: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Thonny\Lib\site-packages\thonny\`).
Full table: [references/api-5.0.1.md](references/api-5.0.1.md).

## Gotchas

- Thonny runs the file **on disk**, not the editor buffer — a "run this"
  feature must save first (`save_all_named_editors()`), or it executes
  stale code.
- `WorkbenchClose` fires **only** on window close (`workbench.py:_on_close`
  is its sole `event_generate`). Cleanup bound to it never runs otherwise;
  files your plugin writes are never auto-removed while Thonny lives.
- **Two localhost listeners on one Thonny pid is normal.** Thonny's own
  single-instance IPC server binds `127.0.0.1:0` (`_create_server_socket`).
  It accepts-then-hangs on HTTP and logs `ast.literal_eval` errors for
  `GET /ping` in `frontend.log`. Don't mistake it for your server, and
  don't probe unknown localhost ports with HTTP unless you accept log spam.
- Windows liveness: `os.kill(pid, 0)` raises `WinError 87` even for **live**
  GUI processes of the same user — it cannot distinguish them from dead
  PIDs. Probe with `ctypes` `OpenProcess(PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION)`:
  non-NULL handle (or access-denied) = alive, NULL + error 87 = dead.
- Breakpoints mirror gutter clicks: `tag_add("breakpoint_line", ...)` on the
  code view text + `update_gutter()`; skip blank/`#` lines; read back with
  `editors.get_current_breakpoints()`.

# Timestamp

An in-session mode that prints the current time, with the delta since the last printed
time, at the start and/or end of each turn. Off until the user turns it on. There is no
storage: the current mode and time zone are whatever the most recent `/timestamp`
command and time-zone line in *this* conversation set (scan back for them).

## The command

`/timestamp <arg>` arrives in the message text or as a slash command with arguments.
Arguments are case-insensitive:

| Argument | Mode |
|---|---|
| `start` / `end` | that one |
| `both`, `on`, `enable` | `both` |
| `off`, `none`, `disable` | `off` |
| *(none)* | `end` |

Reply on that turn, in this order:

1. `Timestamps <enabled|disabled> at <start|end|start and end> of turn.` ("disabled" only
   for `off`, naming the mode being turned off; "start and end" for `both`).
2. Only when the mode goes from `off` to on, the time-zone line (below).
3. The new mode's checks for this same turn: a start check now if it includes `start`, an
   end check at the close if it includes `end`. `off` means no checks on that turn.

Asked which mode is active? Say it; don't run a time check for that.

## Time zone

Chosen once, when the mode goes from `off` to on:

- Known from the user's saved preferences, instructions or this conversation:
  `Using your preferred time zone <TZ>. To change, just request a different time zone.`
- Otherwise UTC:
  `Using default UTC for timestamp time zone. To change, just request a different time zone.`

The user can switch at any time in plain words ("use Pacific time"): acknowledge in one
line and use the new zone from then on.

## Reading the time

Never print a time you did not just read from a tool. Sources, per conversation:

1. A dedicated time tool, if your tool list has one (e.g. `user_time_v0` in the Claude
   mobile app). Try it once; if it fails or is absent, don't try it again this session.
2. Any shell or code-execution tool (`Bash`, `bash_tool`, a terminal), with the zone as an
   IANA name: `TZ=America/Los_Angeles date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z %s'` (the last field is
   epoch seconds, for the delta).

- Compute deltas from epoch seconds, not by subtracting clock strings.
- Never use the date in your system prompt or context: it has no time of day and may be
  in another zone.
- Write the time into your reply text; tool output is often hidden from the user.
- No source available: print `[no time source available this turn]`.

## Format and placement

```
[2026-08-01 14:32:07 PDT, +00:03:12]
[2026-08-01 14:32:07 PDT, first check]
```

- Own line, square brackets, zone label always shown.
- Delta `+HH:MM:SS` since the last printed timestamp; past 24 hours `+Nd HH:MM:SS`.
- `first check` instead of a delta for the conversation's first one.
- `start`: the very first thing in the turn, before any other text or tool call (on the
  `/timestamp` turn itself, right after lines 1-2 above).
- `end`: the very last thing, after all other content and tool calls.
- `both`: both; the end check's delta is measured from the start check.

## Self-check

If the mode is on and the previous turn is missing a check it should have had, or shows a
time that wasn't read from a tool, re-read this skill and follow it strictly from now on.


```
  ERRATA.md                     known doc mistakes (hand-maintained, never refreshed)

    manifest.json               per page: url, md_url, etag, sha256 (LF-normalized), fetched
```

## `scripts/refresh_references.py`

`python .agents/skills/opencode-build/scripts/refresh_references.py [--check] [--force] [--prune]`

1. Fetch `docs/llms.txt`, take the links under `## Build` (up to the next `## `).
   The page list comes from the index, so new pages are picked up automatically.
2. For each page, a GET on its `.md` URL with `If-None-Match: <manifest etag>`
   (skipped with `--force`). `304` -> unchanged. `200` -> LF-normalize, sha256,
   write only if the hash differs (`newline="\n"`, UTF-8).
3. Pages in the manifest but no longer in the index -> reported as removed;
   deleted only with `--prune`.
4. Update `manifest.json` (sorted keys, stable output -> clean diffs).
5. Print a summary: new / updated / removed / unchanged. For every updated page
   that has `ERRATA.md` entries, print "re-check errata: <ids>".
6. `--check`: no writes; exit 1 if anything would change (so a human or a
   scheduled job can see staleness). Network errors exit 2 with the URL.
7. Structure: pure functions (`parse_section`, `page_file`, `normalize`,
   `plan_updates`) plus one injectable `fetch(url, etag)`, so tests run offline.
   Generic User-Agent, no credentials. urllib honors `HTTPS_PROXY`.

## E01: `editor.namespace()` alone does not namespace a tool; id vs Code Mode path
- Page: `plugins-server.md` (section "Tools", the `ctx.tool.transform` example)
- Docs say: the example calls `editor.namespace({ name: "acme", ... })` and adds a
  tool with `options: { namespace: "acme", codemode: true }`, then: "Use `update`
  and `remove` with the effective tool name, including its namespace
  (`acme_greeting` above)." It never says which of the two calls makes the
  prefix, or how the model then sees the tool.
- Actually:
  - Only `options.namespace` on each `editor.add(...)` puts a tool in a
    namespace. Effective id = `<namespace, "." -> "_">_<name>`; without
    `options.namespace` the id is just the name. `editor.namespace()` only
    records a namespace's description (shown in the Code Mode catalog) and
    prefixes nothing. Declaring the namespace and omitting the option gives
    an un-prefixed id: `enter`, not `tutor_enter`.
  - `codemode` is on unless set to `false`. A Code Mode tool is called by the
    model inside Code Mode as `tools.<namespace>.<name>(...)` (dots), or
    `tools.<name>(...)` with no namespace; `pinned: true` lists it up front in
    that catalog. So one tool has two names: id `tutor_enter`
    (`list`/`get`/`update`/`remove`) and Code Mode path `tools.tutor.enter()`.
  - For a plain, direct tool call set `codemode: false`, as opencode's own
    direct tools (bash, patch, question) do. While Code Mode (the `execute`
    tool) is allowed, the model's direct tool list holds only
    `codemode: false` tools; the rest are reachable only through Code Mode.
    If `execute` is denied by permissions, every tool is direct.
  - `ctx.tool.hook("execute.before" | "execute.after")` also fire for calls
    made from Code Mode, and `event.tool` is always the effective id
    (`tutor_enter`, `thonny-agent_eval`), never the bare name or the dotted
    Code Mode path. MCP tools are namespaced by server name
    (`<server>_<tool>`, unsupported characters -> `_`).
- Evidence: opencode v2.2.5 server (`opencode serve`) with a probe plugin;
  `ctx.tool.list()` returned:
  `namespace()` + no option -> id `enter_declared_only`;
  `options: { namespace: "tutor" }` -> `tutor_enter_with_option`;
  `options: { namespace: "tutor", codemode: false }` -> `tutor_enter_direct`.
  The server's bundled source names ids with
  `options?.namespace === undefined ? name : ns.replaceAll(".", "_") + "_" + name`
  and Code Mode paths with `ns + "." + name`, and tells models to call tools as
  `tools.<ns>.<tool>(...)`. Seen in practice: a tool added without the option
  showed up as `tools.enter()`. The direct-list filter and the hook names
  come from the server's tool snapshot and `Tool.execute` code.
- Checked: 2026-11-08 against @opencode/plugin 2.2.5 (opencode v2.2.5)

additions to them. Using the docs needs none of this.

## Downloaded pages

- `references/*.md` (except `*.local.md`) are verbatim copies of the opencode

  page's URL, ETag and hash; a test compares the files with it.
- Refresh: `python scripts/refresh_references.py` (path relative to this
  skill's folder). `--check` reports staleness without writing, `--force`
  ignores ETags, `--prune` deletes pages no longer listed. It prints
  `re-check errata: <ids>` when a page with `ERRATA.md` entries changed.
- Docs contradict the installed types or real behavior: add an entry to
  `ERRATA.md` (its format is at the top of that file), not to the page.

## Local additions: `references/X.local.md`

Our own material for the vendored page `X.md`. The refresh script never
touches these; a test requires the matching `X.md`.

### Where

- Under a copy of the vendor heading of the section supplemented
  (`### Context`, `## Create a client`), so the two files line up.
- Applies to both the client and plugins (same method on `client.<group>`
  and `ctx.<domain>`): `client.local.md`.
- Applies only to plugins: `plugins-server.local.md`, ending with a pointer
  to the client notes for members of the same name.

### File header

What it supplements, that it is not from the docs site, what it was written
from (package and version, e.g. `@opencode/client@2.2.5` `.d.ts`), and that
the installed types win after an upgrade. Then a "Code" line: where each
package lives in the opencode repo at that tag (`@opencode/client` is
`packages/client/`) and the files the reader most likely wants next.

### Code pointers

Name the source file beside each import path, in Reference block comments
(`// @opencode/client/promise/api (packages/client/src/promise/api.ts)`) and
in notes on behavior (`packages/core/src/session/inbox.ts`). Paths are
relative to the opencode repo root at the tag named in the header.

### Reference sections

- One `ts` block of the real declarations, with their real exported names
  (`AgentDomain`, not the vendor's `AgentContext`) and import paths.
- Generate rather than retype (see Tools). Simplify only what is unreadable
  (e.g. a signature listing every event name) and mark it `// simplified`.

### Notes sections

- Non-obvious members only. Most do what group + name say (`list`, `get`,
  `compact`, `switchAgent`); skip them.
- Explain the oddballs: an ambiguous name (`context`: messages? the literal
  context? an object?), a surprising return value (`prompt` returns the
  inbox item, not a result), side effects or costs (prompt cache), limits.
- Group similar members on one line instead of one bullet each.
- Terse: drop the words a reader can predict, keep the ones they can't. One
  or two lines per item; short clauses, `→` for "returns", no filler.
  Still readable without the code beside it.
- Say what is covered so far ("Coverage so far: `session`").
- Behavior that the `.d.ts` files don't show: name the source, e.g.
  "opencode 2.2.5 `packages/core/src/session/instruction-state.ts`" or an
  API operation id.

# Effect

`@opencode/client/effect` is the Effect-native client for the OpenCode HTTP API. It returns typed Effects and Streams
and decodes responses into OpenCode schema values.

```sh
bun add @opencode/client effect@4.0.1
```

## Create a client

Create a client with the server URL, then call methods grouped by API resource.

```ts
import { AbsolutePath, Location, OpenCode } from "@opencode/client/effect"
import { Effect } from "effect"
import { FetchHttpClient } from "effect/http"

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const client = yield* OpenCode.make({ baseUrl: "http://localhost:4096" })
  const session = yield* client.session.create({
    location: Location.Ref.make({ directory: AbsolutePath.make("/workspace") }),
  })
  yield* client.session.prompt({
    sessionID: session.id,
    text: "Review the current changes",
  })
  return session
})

const session = await Effect.runPromise(program.pipe(Effect.provide(FetchHttpClient.layer)))
```

## Headers and requests

Configure default headers on the supplied `HttpClient`. Native operations use
normal Effect interruption for cancellation. RPC methods additionally accept
per-call location, header, and signal options.

{/* prettier-ignore */}
```ts
import { HttpClient, HttpClientRequest } from "effect/http"

const httpClient = yield* HttpClient.HttpClient
const client = yield* OpenCode.make({ baseUrl: "https://opencode.example.com" }).pipe(
  Effect.provideService(
    HttpClient.HttpClient,
    HttpClient.mapRequest(httpClient, (request) =>
      HttpClientRequest.setHeaders(request, { authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.OPENCODE_TOKEN}` }),
    ),
  ),
)

const sessions = yield* client.session.list()
```

## Stream events

Streaming operations such as `event.subscribe()` and `experimental.session.log()` return Effect Streams.

{/* prettier-ignore */}
```ts
import { Effect, Stream } from "effect"

yield* client.event
  .subscribe()
  .pipe(Stream.runForEach((event) => Effect.logInfo("OpenCode event", { type: event.type })))
```

Native and RPC event Streams share one lazy connection per client. Constructing
a Stream does not connect; consuming it does. Stopping one consumer leaves others
running, and the last consumer leaving closes the source. Source EOF or failure
ends current subscriptions without automatic retry or replay. Late native consumers
receive the current connection marker before live events.

## Plugin RPC

Use the same shared contract as Promise clients and server plugins:

{/* prettier-ignore */}
```ts
import { Acme } from "opencode-acme-plugin/rpc"

const acme = client.rpc(Acme)
const result = yield* acme.search({ query: "hello" }, { location: { directory: "/workspace" } })

yield* acme.events
  .subscribe("updated")
  .pipe(
    Stream.runForEach((event) =>
      Effect.logInfo("Plugin event", { type: event.type, location: event.location, text: event.data.text }),
    ),
  )
```

Method arguments and results are inferred from the contract. The second optional
argument holds `location`, `signal`, and `headers`; omitted location uses the
normal request defaults. Calls are interrupted with their consuming Effect.
Method error maps are inferred in the Effect error channel. Declared errors are
decoded through their data schemas. The typed subclient removes the generic HTTP
RPC error wrapper; reserved `rpc.*` types identify framework failures.

RPC events are typed Streams, not callback-style `on` listeners. They receive the
RPC's events from all locations, each with required `location` and a normal
prefixed type such as `rpc.acme.updated`. This differs from server-plugin handles,
which are fixed to their own location. See [Effect plugin RPC](/build/plugins/effect/rpc) for
definitions, schemas, registration, and live subscription semantics.

## Local background service

The Node-only `@opencode/client/effect/service` entrypoint discovers, starts, authenticates, and stops the local
background service as Effects.

```sh
bun add @effect/platform-node@4.0.1
```

Create an authenticated client for the ensured service.

```ts
import { NodeFileSystem } from "@effect/platform-node"
import { OpenCode } from "@opencode/client/effect"
import { Service } from "@opencode/client/effect/service"
import { Effect } from "effect"
import { FetchHttpClient, HttpClient, HttpClientRequest } from "effect/http"

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const endpoint = yield* Service.ensure()
  const httpClient = yield* HttpClient.HttpClient
  const client = yield* OpenCode.make({ baseUrl: endpoint.url }).pipe(
    Effect.provideService(
      HttpClient.HttpClient,
      HttpClient.mapRequest(httpClient, (request) =>
        HttpClientRequest.setHeaders(request, Service.headers(endpoint) ?? {}),
      ),
    ),
  )
  return yield* client.server.info()
})

const health = await Effect.runPromise(
  program.pipe(Effect.provide(FetchHttpClient.layer), Effect.provide(NodeFileSystem.layer)),
)
```

Discover without starting, or stop the exact registered service.

{/* prettier-ignore */}
```ts
const endpoint = yield* Service.discover()
yield* Service.stop()
```

# JavaScript

`@opencode/client` is the TypeScript client for the OpenCode HTTP
API. Use it when your application connects to an OpenCode server over the
network. Its native types and methods are generated from the same contract as the
[API reference](/api). Plugin RPC types come from imported RPC definitions.

## Install

```sh
bun add @opencode/client
```

## Create a client

Create a client with the server URL, then call methods grouped by API resource:

```ts
import { OpenCode } from "@opencode/client"

const client = OpenCode.make({
  baseUrl: "http://localhost:4096",
})

const session = await client.session.create({
  location: { directory: "/workspace" },
})

await client.session.prompt({
  sessionID: session.id,
  text: "Review the current changes",
})
```

## Headers and requests

Pass default authentication or application headers to `OpenCode.make` with
`headers`. You can also supply a custom `fetch` implementation. Each operation
accepts request options as its final argument for an `AbortSignal` or
per-request headers. Event subscriptions are the exception: they accept only
subscriber-local cancellation and use the base client's headers.

```ts
const client = OpenCode.make({
  baseUrl: "https://opencode.example.com",
  headers: {
    authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.OPENCODE_TOKEN}`,
  },
})

await client.session.list(undefined, {
  signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000),
})
```

## Stream events

Streaming endpoints return async iterables:

```ts
for await (const event of client.event.subscribe()) {
  console.log(event.type)
}
```

Native and RPC event subscribers share one lazy connection per client. Client,
handle, and iterable creation open no event connection; consumption starts it.
Breaking iteration or aborting a subscriber ends only that iterator. The last
subscriber leaving closes the connection. The shared source waits for active
subscribers to accept each event; consumers should buffer before performing slow work.

Subscriptions are live-only, with no replay or automatic reconnection. A source
failure ends current subscriptions; subscribe again after recovery. A late native
subscriber receives the current `server.connected` marker, not past business events.

Pass `types` to receive only some event types. The events are typed to match, and
`server.connected` always comes through so a filtered subscriber still knows when to resync.
Filtering happens on the shared connection, inside the client.

```ts
for await (const event of client.event.subscribe({ types: ["config.updated"] })) {
  // event.type is "config.updated" | "server.connected"
}
```

## Plugin RPC

Import a plugin's shared contract and pass it to `client.rpc`:

```ts
import { OpenCode } from "@opencode/client"
import { Acme } from "opencode-acme-plugin/rpc"

const acme = client.rpc(Acme)
const result = await acme.search(
  { query: "hello" },
  { location: { directory: "/workspace" }, signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000) },
)

const unsubscribe = acme.events.on("updated", (event) => {
  console.log(event.type, event.location.directory, event.data.text)
})
```

The second optional method argument holds `location`, `signal`, and `headers`,
separate from the plugin-defined input. Omitted location follows native request
defaults: base location headers, then the server's working directory. No location
is selected when constructing the subclient.

Methods infer arguments and results from the definition. Schema parsing belongs
to the contract boundary; callers send the accepted input representation, while
handlers receive parsed values. The Promise client accepts Standard Schema or
plain JSON Schema definitions and does
not run schema parsers locally: the server returns already parsed and transformed
output. Effect Schema definitions require the Effect client.

Declared method errors reject like errors from other Promise client endpoints,
and caught errors remain untyped. Generic HTTP RPC error wrappers are removed by
the typed subclient. Reserved `rpc.*` framework failures remain plain RPC failures,
while unrelated authentication, transport, and protocol errors keep their normal
client representations.

RPC subscriptions use local names and receive that RPC's events across all
locations. Inspect the required `event.location` to filter them. `events.subscribe`
matches the native async iterable API:

```ts
for await (const event of acme.events.subscribe("updated")) {
  console.log(event.data.text)
}
```

`events.on` is a convenience wrapper over the same source. It returns unsubscribe;
async callbacks are awaited sequentially. Callback or source failures are logged
and end that listener. Native and typed subscriptions receive the same normal
`rpc.<rpcID>.<event>` envelope with direct object event data. Live subscriptions
do not replay missed events.

The server plugin must be configured and implement the RPC; importing a
definition does not register it. See [plugin RPC](/build/plugins/rpc) for the
definition and registration API. Any HTTP client can also invoke the generic
`POST /api/rpc/{rpcID}/{method}` route with `{ "input": ... }` and receive
`{ "output": ... }`. Omitted input/output fields represent no value.

## Local background service

The main client entrypoints are browser-compatible and do not include local
process management. In a Node application, import the native Promise service
API from `@opencode/client/service`.

- `Service.discover()` returns a healthy registered endpoint without starting
  a process.
- `Service.ensure()` returns a compatible service, starting one when needed.
- `Service.stop()` stops the exact registered service instance.
- `Service.headers(endpoint)` creates the authentication headers for a client.

```ts
import { OpenCode } from "@opencode/client"
import { Service } from "@opencode/client/service"

const endpoint = await Service.ensure()
const client = OpenCode.make({
  baseUrl: endpoint.url,
  headers: Service.headers(endpoint),
})

const info = await client.server.info()
```

`Service.ensure()` accepts an optional registration file, version, service
command, and `onStart` callback. `version` accepts either an exact value or a
compatibility predicate:

```ts
const endpoint = await Service.ensure({
  file: "/var/run/opencode/service.json",
  version: (version) => version.startsWith("2."),
  command: ["opencode", "serve", "--service"],
  onStart(reason, previousVersion) {
    console.log(reason, previousVersion)
  },
})
```

Omit these options to use the standard registration path and
`opencode serve --service` command.

# TUI

TUI plugins extend the terminal UI with commands, routes, slots, Markdown renderers, notifications, and local state. A
TUI plugin is the `./tui` part of a [plugin package](/build/plugins), usually beside a [server
part](/build/plugins/server).

```ts title="src/tui.tsx"
import { Plugin } from "@opencode/plugin/tui"

export default Plugin.define({
  id: "acme.cli",
  setup(context) {
    context.ui.toast.show({ message: "TUI plugin loaded", variant: "success" })
  },
})
```

Import `@opencode/plugin/tui` directly. OpenCode resolves this import at runtime, so local TUI plugins do not need an
absolute path to an OpenCode checkout.

## Context

`setup` receives configuration, app metadata, the current location, the OpenCode client, cached data, theme tokens, the
OpenTUI renderer, and the UI APIs documented below.

```ts
setup(context) {
  const compact = context.options.compact === true
  const location = context.location ?? context.data.location.default()
  const version = context.app.version
  const channel = context.app.channel
  const client = context.client
  const renderer = context.renderer
  const theme = context.theme
}
```

Return a cleanup function for resources owned by the plugin.

```ts
setup(context) {
  const stop = context.data.on("session.execution.succeeded", () => {})
  return () => stop()
}
```

## Client

`context.client` is the generated OpenCode client and can call the connected server, including a remote server.

```ts
const response = await context.client.plugin.list({
  location: context.location ?? context.data.location.default(),
})
const plugins = response.data
```

## Events

Use `data.on` for one typed event or `data.listen` for every server event; both return an unsubscribe function.

```ts
const stopPermission = context.data.on("permission.asked", (event) => {
  context.ui.toast.show({ message: `Permission ${event.data.id}` })
})
const stopAll = context.data.listen(({ details }) => console.log(details.type))

return () => {
  stopPermission()
  stopAll()
}
```

## Sessions

Session data exposes list, lookup, hierarchy, cost, status, synchronization, and invalidation.

```ts
const sessions = context.data.session.list()
const session = context.data.session.get(sessionID)
const rootID = context.data.session.root(sessionID)
const familyIDs = context.data.session.family(sessionID)
const cost = context.data.session.cost(sessionID)
const status = context.data.session.status(sessionID)
await context.data.session.sync(sessionID)
context.data.session.invalidate(sessionID)
```

Pending inbox items and messages have list, lookup, sync, and invalidate APIs.

```ts
await context.data.session.pending.sync(sessionID)
const pending = context.data.session.pending.list(sessionID)
context.data.session.pending.invalidate(sessionID)

await context.data.session.message.sync(sessionID)
const messages = context.data.session.message.list(sessionID)
const message = context.data.session.message.get(sessionID, messageID)
context.data.session.message.invalidate(sessionID)
```

Permission requests can be read and refreshed for a session.

```ts
await context.data.session.permission.sync(sessionID)
const requests = context.data.session.permission.list(sessionID) ?? []
context.data.session.permission.invalidate(sessionID)
```

Forms can be listed, refreshed, replied to, or cancelled at a location.

```ts
import type { SessionFormCancelInput, SessionFormReplyInput } from "@opencode/client"

async function handleForm(reply: SessionFormReplyInput, cancel: SessionFormCancelInput) {
  const location = context.location
  await context.data.session.form.sync(sessionID, location)
  const forms = context.data.session.form.list(sessionID, location) ?? []
  await context.data.session.form.reply(reply, location)
  await context.data.session.form.cancel(cancel, location)
  context.data.session.form.invalidate(sessionID, location)
}
```

```ts
await context.data.project.permission.sync(projectID)

context.data.project.permission.invalidate(projectID)
```

```ts
await context.data.shell.sync(context.location)
```

```ts
const result = await context.attention.notify({
  title: "OpenCode",
  message: "Session done",
  notification: { when: "blurred" },
  sound: { name: "done", volume: 0.5, when: "always" },

console.log(result.ok, result.notification, result.sound, result.skipped)
```

## Theme and renderer

Use semantic theme tokens with OpenTUI elements and pass `context.renderer` to renderer-specific helpers.

```tsx
const Status = () => <text fg={context.theme.text.base}>Ready</text>
const renderer = context.renderer
```

An OpenTUI resource that the renderer draws needs `context.renderer.nativeScene` as its owner. For example, `<markdown>`
and `<code>` need a `SyntaxStyle`. Destroy the resource when the renderer is idle, after the last frame that draws it.

```tsx
import { SyntaxStyle } from "@opentui/core"

const style = SyntaxStyle.fromStyles({ default: { fg: context.theme.text.base } }, context.renderer.nativeScene)
context.ui.slot({ append: "home.footer", render: () => <markdown content="Ready" syntaxStyle={style} /> })
return () => context.renderer.idle().then(() => style.destroy())
```

To read the layout style of a renderable, call the method with the Yoga Node getter's name, such as
`box.getPadding(Yoga.Edge.Bottom)` or `box.getMaxWidth()`. Host renderables are not part of the plugin API. Their
structure and styles can change in any release.

### Plugins built for OpenTUI 0.5

OpenCode runs plugins with its own OpenTUI. Since OpenTUI 0.6:

- `SyntaxStyle.create()`, `SyntaxStyle.fromStyles()`, `SyntaxStyle.fromTheme()`, `TextBuffer.create()`, and
  `EditBuffer.create()` take an owner as their last argument. `OptimizedBuffer.create()` takes it in the `owner` option.
  Pass `context.renderer.nativeScene`. OpenTUI 0.5 ignores the extra argument, so the plugin still runs on older
  OpenCode releases.
- `generateSyntax()` from `@opencode/theme/tui` takes the owner as its second argument:
  `generateSyntax(context.theme, context.renderer.nativeScene)`. Older `@opencode/theme` versions build the style
  without an owner, so update the package too.
- `getLayoutNode()` is removed. Replace `getLayoutNode().getMaxWidth()` and the other style getters with the
  renderable method of the same name, on OpenTUI 0.6.5 or later. Replace `getComputedLayout()` and the other computed
  position and size getters with `getLayout()`, and `markDirty()` with `invalidateIntrinsicSize()`. Computed padding,
  margin, and border have no replacement, and `getPadding(edge)` reads only the padding set for that edge. To restore a
  style that a getter reports as unset (`Unit.Undefined`), assign `undefined` to the property, on OpenTUI 0.6.6 or
  later.

The [OpenTUI 0.6.0 release notes](https://opentui.com/docs/releases/0.6.0) list every change.

```ts
const unregister = context.markdown.registerCodeBlockRenderer("acme", (_token, render) => render.defaultRender())
return unregister
```
